interactions.label: Which statement about the American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) physical s

params.question: Which statement about the American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) physical status classification is correct?

answers.text: It grades the severity of the patient's systemic disease, with an E suffix for emergency surgery

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. ASA grades the patient's systemic illness before surgery, so it tells you how much preparation and monitoring this person needs. The E suffix flags emergency cases, where there is less time for optimisation.

answers.text: It grades the technical difficulty of the planned operation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Wrong. ASA grades the patient, not the operation. Operative complexity is a separate consideration, and conflating the two leads to under- or over-preparing the patient.

answers.text: It assesses airway anatomy and is the same as the Mallampati score

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Wrong. This describes the Mallampati classification, which assesses airway anatomy. The two are separate systems and must not be conflated.

answers.text: ASA VI denotes a patient with mild systemic disease undergoing elective surgery

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Wrong. ASA VI is a brain-dead organ donor. Mild systemic disease is ASA II. Learn the endpoints first: I is a normal healthy patient, VI is brain-dead.

overallFeedback.feedback: Not quite. ASA physical status grades the patient's systemic illness (I to VI, with E for emergency). It does not grade the operation or the airway. Revisit the preoperative sequence.
Correct. ASA grades the severity of systemic disease before surgery, and the E suffix marks emergency cases. Keep it separate from the Mallampati airway grade.

interactions.label: A 70-year-old man is booked for hernia repair. His daughter answers most of the

params.question: A 70-year-old man is booked for hernia repair. His daughter answers most of the surgeon's questions for him and says he will agree to whatever the family decides. He then signs the consent form while she stands beside him. Which pillar of valid consent is most clearly compromised?

answers.text: Capacity: older adults are presumed to lack it, so the signature is invalid

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Wrong. Capacity is presumed in adults and is decision-specific. Age alone is not evidence of incapacity, and an unwise choice does not prove it either.

answers.text: Voluntariness: the decision must be his own, free from pressure by family

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Voluntariness means the patient decides for himself, free from pressure by family, employer or the team. A daughter answering for him and steering the decision puts this pillar at risk.

answers.text: Disclosure: a signed form proves the risks were explained, so there is no gap

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Wrong. A signed form records the conversation; it does not replace it. The disclosure pillar requires the material risks, benefits and alternatives to be explained to the patient himself.

answers.text: Nothing: once a signed consent form is on file, the consent is valid

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Wrong. Consent is a process, not a form. A signature without capacity, voluntariness and genuine disclosure is not valid consent.

overallFeedback.feedback: Not quite. Check the three pillars: capacity, voluntariness and disclosure. The key question is whose decision it is.
Correct. Valid consent rests on capacity, voluntariness and disclosure. Here the decision is not clearly the patient's own, so the consent process must be repeated with him alone.

interactions.label: While retracting, you notice your glove has torn near the thumb. What should you

params.question: While retracting, you notice your glove has torn near the thumb. What should you do?

answers.text: Tape the tear and finish the retraction, since the surgeon needs you at the table

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Wrong. Taping does not restore sterility. A torn glove is a breach, so the hand and any contacted area must be treated as contaminated.

answers.text: Re-glove immediately, since a torn glove means the hand is no longer sterile

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A breach of the glove makes the hand non-sterile, and the sterile field depends on every gloved hand being intact. Re-glove immediately, and re-gown if your gown is also compromised.

answers.text: Continue, since a small tear still covers the hand

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Wrong. Any tear, however small, lets contamination reach the skin. Sterility is all or nothing for the glove.

answers.text: Wait for the surgeon to finish the step, then change gloves before closing

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Wrong. Contamination must be corrected immediately, not at a convenient pause. Continuing to work with a breached glove risks surgical site infection.

overallFeedback.feedback: Not quite. Under the sterile-movement rules, a torn glove or suspected contamination must be corrected immediately by re-gloving or re-gowning.
Correct. Any glove tear or suspected contamination requires immediate re-gloving, and re-gowning if needed. Sterility is restored only by replacing the breached item.

interactions.label: On day 1 after a laparotomy, a patient's heart rate has risen steadily over four

params.question: On day 1 after a laparotomy, a patient's heart rate has risen steadily over four hours and the pulse pressure is narrowing. Her blood pressure is still within the normal range. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

answers.text: Normal recovery: the normal blood pressure is reassuring, so routine observations are enough

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Wrong. A normal early blood pressure is falsely reassuring. Hypotension appears only after more than 30% of blood volume is lost, so the trend is the warning.

answers.text: Early haemorrhage: escalate now, because hypotension is a late sign

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A rising heart rate with a narrowing pulse pressure signals early bleeding before any fall in blood pressure. Read the trend against the postoperative day and escalate early.

answers.text: Pain alone: give more analgesia and reassess in 12 hours

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Wrong. Pain can raise the heart rate, but a trend with narrowing pulse pressure must be treated as possible bleeding until excluded. Waiting 12 hours risks missing it.

answers.text: Anaesthetic drug effect that will resolve without escalation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Wrong. Residual anaesthetic effects do not explain a rising heart rate with narrowing pulse pressure on a postoperative day. Treat the trend as a deterioration until proven otherwise.

overallFeedback.feedback: Not quite. Postoperative deterioration follows trends, not single values. Hypotension is a late sign, so a normal blood pressure does not rule out early haemorrhage.
Correct. Postoperative deterioration shows in trends: rising heart rate and narrowing pulse pressure precede hypotension and signal early bleeding.
